title: Bar Exam: Contracts and UCC Article 2

sources.name: Original educational synthesis from general knowledge
Cornell LII: public UCC Article 2 reference; original summaries

description: For bar candidates reviewing general U.S. common-law contracts and traditional UCC Article 2 rules. State enactments and exceptions vary; verify with current guidelines.

cards.front: What is a contract?
cards.back: An agreement creating obligations enforceable by law.

cards.front: What law generally governs service contracts?
cards.back: State common law, subject to applicable statutes.

cards.front: What transactions does UCC Article 2 principally govern?
cards.back: Sales of goods.

cards.front: What are goods under Article 2?
cards.back: Movable things identified to the sales contract, subject to statutory exclusions such as the money used to pay the price.

cards.front: How do many courts classify a mixed goods-and-services contract?
cards.back: They apply the predominant-purpose test; some jurisdictions instead focus on the source of the particular claim.

cards.front: What is the objective theory of assent?
cards.back: Agreement is judged by reasonably understood outward words and conduct, not undisclosed intentions.

cards.front: What is an offer?
cards.back: A communication showing willingness to bargain that reasonably indicates acceptance will complete the agreement.

cards.front: Are ordinary advertisements usually offers?
cards.back: Usually not; they generally invite offers. Definite commitments, such as some reward advertisements, can be offers.

cards.front: What distinguishes a price quote from an offer?
cards.back: A quote often supplies information; it becomes an offer only when its terms and context reasonably invite acceptance to conclude a bargain.

cards.front: What is acceptance?
cards.back: Assent to an offer in the manner it invites or requires.

cards.front: What is a bilateral contract?
cards.back: A contract formed through an exchange of promises.

cards.front: What is a unilateral contract?
cards.back: A contract accepted by the requested performance rather than a return promise.

cards.front: What is the common-law mirror-image rule?
cards.back: A purported acceptance that conditions assent on changed terms is a counteroffer rather than an acceptance.

cards.front: Does a request for a better price always reject an offer?
cards.back: No. A mere inquiry can leave the original offer open.

cards.front: What is a counteroffer?
cards.back: A proposed substitute bargain that generally terminates the power to accept the original offer, subject to exceptions.

cards.front: When is revocation ordinarily effective?
cards.back: When communicated to the offeree before acceptance, unless the offer is irrevocable.

cards.front: What is indirect revocation?
cards.back: Reliable information that the offeror has taken action inconsistent with continuing the offer can terminate the offeree's power of acceptance.

cards.front: When does an offer lapse if it sets no deadline?
cards.back: After a reasonable time under the circumstances.

cards.front: What generally happens to an ordinary offer when the offeror dies before acceptance?
cards.back: The power of acceptance terminates, even without the offeree's knowledge; option contracts are treated differently.

cards.front: What is an option contract?
cards.back: A binding agreement that limits the offeror's power to revoke an offer for a specified period.

cards.front: What ordinarily supports a common-law option?
cards.back: Consideration for the promise to keep the offer open, or a recognized substitute under applicable law.

cards.front: What protection may beginning invited unilateral performance create?
cards.back: An option that prevents revocation while the offeree has a reasonable opportunity to complete performance.

cards.front: Does mere preparation necessarily count as beginning unilateral performance?
cards.back: No. Preparation is distinct from the invited performance, though reliance doctrines may protect some preparations.

cards.front: What is the usual mailbox rule?
cards.back: A properly dispatched acceptance by an authorized medium is generally effective on dispatch, subject to exceptions.

cards.front: When is acceptance of an option ordinarily effective?
cards.back: On receipt by the offeror, unless the option provides otherwise.

cards.front: Can an offer require receipt of acceptance?
cards.back: Yes. Its terms can displace the default mailbox rule.

cards.front: Is silence ordinarily acceptance?
cards.back: No. Exceptions can arise from prior dealings, accepted benefits with reason to expect payment, or other recognized circumstances.

cards.front: Must an offeree know of a reward offer before accepting it by performance?
cards.back: Generally yes; the performance must be undertaken with knowledge of the offer.

cards.front: What is consideration?
cards.back: A bargained-for exchange of a promise, act, forbearance, or other legally sufficient detriment.

cards.front: Do courts usually measure whether consideration is economically equal?
cards.back: No. They usually examine legal sufficiency rather than equivalent value, though other defenses may apply.

cards.front: Why is past consideration usually insufficient?
cards.back: The past act was not bargained for in exchange for the later promise.

cards.front: What is the preexisting-duty rule?
cards.back: Doing only what one already legally owes the promisor ordinarily does not supply new consideration for a modification.

cards.front: Can surrendering a disputed claim be consideration?
cards.back: Yes, when the claim is doubtful in fact or law or asserted in good faith under the applicable rule.

cards.front: What is an illusory promise?
cards.back: Language that leaves performance entirely optional and imposes no real commitment.

cards.front: Why are good-faith requirements contracts not ordinarily illusory?
cards.back: The buyer commits to its actual good-faith requirements, with statutory limits on disproportionate demands.

cards.front: What is promissory estoppel?
cards.back: Enforcement based on a promise reasonably inducing foreseeable detrimental reliance when enforcement is needed to prevent injustice.

cards.front: Must a promissory-estoppel remedy always equal full expectation damages?
cards.back: No. Relief may be limited as justice requires.

cards.front: What is restitution primarily intended to prevent?
cards.back: Unjust enrichment at another person's expense.

cards.front: What is an implied-in-fact contract?
cards.back: An actual agreement inferred from conduct rather than express words.

cards.front: What is a quasi-contract claim?
cards.back: A restitutionary obligation imposed by law, even without an actual agreement.

cards.front: What does voidable mean?
cards.back: A party entitled to avoid the transaction can choose to affirm or disaffirm it.

cards.front: What is the usual contract rule for minors?
cards.back: Their contracts are generally voidable, subject to exceptions and jurisdiction-specific rules.

cards.front: What is the general necessaries exception for minors?
cards.back: A minor may owe restitution for the reasonable value of necessary goods or services, depending on circumstances and state law.

cards.front: How can an adult ratify a contract made during minority?
cards.back: By affirming it after reaching majority, including through conduct recognized by the jurisdiction.

cards.front: When can mental incapacity make a contract voidable?
cards.back: When the person cannot understand its nature and consequences, or under an applicable rule cannot act reasonably and the other party has reason to know.

cards.front: What makes a contract voidable for intoxication under the usual rule?
cards.back: The other party has reason to know that intoxication prevents understanding or reasonable action regarding the transaction.

cards.front: What is economic duress?
cards.back: An improper threat that induces assent while leaving no reasonable alternative.

cards.front: What is undue influence?
cards.back: Unfair persuasion of a person under domination or in a relationship that justifies special trust.

cards.front: What kind of misrepresentation can justify avoidance?
cards.back: A fraudulent or material misrepresentation that induces justified reliance, subject to applicable requirements.

cards.front: What is mutual mistake?
cards.back: Both parties share an erroneous belief about a basic assumption that materially affects the exchange.

cards.front: When may mutual mistake support avoidance?
cards.back: When the mistake materially affects the agreed exchange and the adversely affected party does not bear the risk.

cards.front: Does unilateral mistake automatically permit rescission?
cards.back: No. Additional requirements apply, such as unconscionable enforcement or the other party's knowledge or causation, plus lack of assumed risk.

cards.front: What is procedural unconscionability?
cards.back: Unfairness in the bargaining process, such as oppressive terms hidden in circumstances of unequal choice.

cards.front: What is substantive unconscionability?
cards.back: Unreasonably harsh or one-sided contract terms.

cards.front: What can a court do with an unconscionable clause?
cards.back: Refuse enforcement, sever it, or limit its application, subject to governing law.

cards.front: What does the Statute of Frauds generally require?
cards.back: Specified kinds of agreements need a sufficient signed writing or a recognized exception to be enforceable.

cards.front: Does the Statute of Frauds generally make an oral agreement criminal?
cards.back: No. It concerns enforceability, not criminality.

cards.front: What is the one-year provision of the Statute of Frauds?
cards.back: It generally covers agreements that cannot by their terms be fully performed within one year of formation.

cards.front: Does an indefinite-duration agreement necessarily fall within the one-year provision?
cards.back: No. The question is possible completion within one year under its terms, not expected duration.

cards.front: What is the land-contract Statute of Frauds category?
cards.back: Contracts transferring an interest in land generally require a signed writing, subject to recognized exceptions.

cards.front: What is the suretyship category of the Statute of Frauds?
cards.back: A promise to answer for another's debt generally requires a writing, subject to exceptions.

cards.front: What is the main-purpose exception in suretyship?
cards.back: A promise primarily serving the promisor's own economic interest may fall outside the suretyship writing requirement.

cards.front: Whose signature generally matters for a Statute of Frauds defense?
cards.back: The signature of the party against whom enforcement is sought, or an authorized agent, subject to exceptions.

cards.front: What is an integrated agreement?
cards.back: A writing adopted as a final expression of some or all agreement terms.

cards.front: What is a completely integrated agreement?
cards.back: A writing intended as the complete and exclusive statement of the agreement's terms.

cards.front: What does the parol evidence rule address?
cards.back: The effect of prior or contemporaneous agreements on the terms of an integrated writing.

cards.front: Does the parol evidence rule bar proof of a later modification?
cards.back: No. Later agreements are outside its basic time scope, though other formalities may apply.

cards.front: Can outside evidence be used to show fraud or duress?
cards.back: Generally yes, subject to jurisdiction-specific limits and the nature of the claim.

cards.front: Can a partially integrated writing be supplemented by consistent additional terms?
cards.back: Generally yes, but it cannot ordinarily be contradicted by prior or contemporaneous agreements.

cards.front: What is an express condition?
cards.back: An event the parties explicitly make a prerequisite to a contractual duty, unless excused.

cards.front: What is a condition precedent?
cards.back: An event that must occur before a duty becomes due, unless excused.

cards.front: How does a promise differ from a condition?
cards.back: Breach of a promise can create liability; nonoccurrence of a condition generally prevents a dependent duty from becoming due.

cards.front: What is substantial performance?
cards.back: Performance close enough to satisfy a constructive condition of exchange despite minor defects, while leaving damages for those defects.

cards.front: Does substantial performance ordinarily replace strict compliance with an express condition?
cards.back: No. Express conditions generally require strict satisfaction unless excused.

cards.front: What is a material breach?
cards.back: A sufficiently serious failure that can excuse the other party's remaining performance, depending on circumstances.

cards.front: What is a minor breach?
cards.back: A breach supporting damages but ordinarily not excusing the other party's remaining duties.

cards.front: What is anticipatory repudiation?
cards.back: A clear indication before performance is due that a party will not perform a material contractual obligation.

cards.front: What options generally follow anticipatory repudiation?
cards.back: The injured party may treat it as breach and seek relief or await performance within the governing limits.

cards.front: When can a repudiating party generally retract?
cards.back: Before the other party materially changes position in reliance or indicates that the repudiation is final, subject to governing rules.

cards.front: What is waiver of a condition?
cards.back: Intentional relinquishment of the right to insist on that condition, as recognized by governing law.

cards.front: What is the prevention doctrine?
cards.back: A party ordinarily cannot rely on failure of a condition that its own wrongful conduct prevented.

cards.front: What is impossibility of performance?
cards.back: A supervening event makes required performance objectively impossible under the applicable doctrine.

cards.front: What is impracticability?
cards.back: An unallocated supervening event makes performance extraordinarily burdensome, not merely less profitable, under a recognized excuse doctrine.

cards.front: What is frustration of purpose?
cards.back: An unallocated supervening event substantially destroys the contract's principal shared purpose, though performance remains possible.

cards.front: Does an ordinary market-price increase usually excuse performance?
cards.back: No. Ordinary market risk is generally allocated to the parties.

cards.front: What is rescission by agreement?
cards.back: The parties agree to discharge their remaining contractual duties.

cards.front: What is an accord?
cards.back: An agreement to accept a different performance in satisfaction of an existing duty.

cards.front: What is satisfaction in accord and satisfaction?
cards.back: Performance of the accord, which discharges the original duty.

cards.front: What is a novation?
cards.back: An agreement substituting a new obligor and releasing the original obligor with the required parties' assent.

cards.front: Does delegation alone release the original obligor?
cards.back: No. A release generally requires a novation or another recognized basis.

cards.front: What is assignment?
cards.back: Transfer of a contractual right to another person.

cards.front: What is delegation?
cards.back: Transfer of responsibility to perform a contractual duty, without necessarily releasing the delegator.

cards.front: When is delegation generally restricted?
cards.back: When the obligee has a substantial interest in the original obligor's personal performance or the contract or law validly prohibits it.

cards.front: Can an assignment materially increase the obligor's burden?
cards.back: An assignment that materially changes the duty, burden, or risk is generally restricted.

cards.front: Who is an intended third-party beneficiary?
cards.back: A nonparty whom the contracting parties intended to have an enforceable benefit under the applicable test.

cards.front: Can an incidental beneficiary ordinarily enforce a contract?
cards.back: No. A merely incidental benefit does not create enforcement rights.

cards.front: When can an intended beneficiary's rights vest under a common rule?
cards.back: Through qualifying assent, material reliance, or suit, subject to contract terms and jurisdictional rules.

cards.front: What is the expectation interest?
cards.back: Putting the injured party in the economic position it would have occupied had the contract been performed.

cards.front: What is the reliance interest?
cards.back: Reimbursing qualifying losses from reliance on the agreement, subject to limits including proof that the bargain would have lost money.

cards.front: What is the restitution interest?
cards.back: Recovering the value of a benefit conferred on the other party, when restitution is available.

cards.front: What limits ordinarily constrain contract damages?
cards.back: Causation, foreseeability, reasonable certainty, and avoidable-loss principles.

cards.front: What is the foreseeability limit on consequential damages?
cards.back: The kind of loss must have been reasonably foreseeable at formation as a probable result of breach.

cards.front: What is mitigation in contract damages?
cards.back: An injured party cannot recover losses reasonably avoidable without undue risk, burden, or humiliation.

cards.front: Are punitive damages normally available for a simple contract breach?
cards.back: No. An independent basis, such as an actionable tort and applicable law, is generally required.

cards.front: When are liquidated damages generally enforceable?
cards.back: When a reasonable preagreed estimate of compensable loss meets applicable requirements and is not an unenforceable penalty.

cards.front: What is specific performance?
cards.back: A court order requiring promised performance, generally when money damages are inadequate and equitable requirements are met.

cards.front: Are courts likely to compel personal services by specific performance?
cards.back: Generally no.

cards.front: Why may land-sale contracts qualify for specific performance?
cards.back: Land is traditionally treated as unique, making money damages potentially inadequate.

cards.front: What is nominal damages relief?
cards.back: A small award recognizing breach when recoverable loss is not established.

cards.front: What is a merchant for Article 2 purposes?
cards.back: A person who deals in goods of the kind or has relevant specialized knowledge or skill; the precise merchant rule depends on the provision.

cards.front: What is the traditional UCC goods Statute of Frauds threshold?
cards.back: A price of $500 or more, subject to exceptions and the applicable state's enactment.

cards.front: What term ordinarily limits enforcement under UCC 2-201's writing rule?
cards.back: The quantity shown in the writing.

cards.front: How long does a merchant have to object to a qualifying written confirmation under UCC 2-201?
cards.back: Ten days after receipt; the objection must be written.

cards.front: Does a merchant confirmation itself conclusively prove an oral contract existed?
cards.back: No. It can overcome the writing defense but does not alone establish the agreement.

cards.front: What is the specially manufactured goods exception to UCC 2-201?
cards.back: Custom goods unsuitable for ordinary resale may qualify after a substantial start or procurement commitment before repudiation, with circumstances indicating the buyer's order.

cards.front: How does an in-court admission affect UCC 2-201?
cards.back: It permits enforcement up to the admitted quantity.

cards.front: How can performance satisfy UCC 2-201?
cards.back: Enforcement is possible for goods accepted after receipt or covered by payment made and accepted.

cards.front: What makes a UCC firm offer irrevocable without consideration?
cards.back: A merchant's signed writing assuring that an offer to buy or sell goods will remain open, subject to statutory limits.

cards.front: What is the maximum UCC firm-offer irrevocability period without consideration?
cards.back: Three months; a shorter stated or reasonable period can apply.

cards.front: What extra formality applies if a firm-offer assurance is on the offeree's form?
cards.back: The offeror must separately sign the assurance term.

cards.front: Does a good-faith UCC modification require new consideration?
cards.back: No, though the Statute of Frauds and valid writing requirements may still apply.

cards.front: Can Article 2 form a contract with open terms?
cards.back: Yes, if intent to contract and a reasonably certain remedy basis exist.

cards.front: What is the usual UCC open-price default?
cards.back: A reasonable price at the time of delivery, when the parties intended to contract despite the gap.

cards.front: What limits quantities in output and requirements contracts?
cards.back: Actual good-faith output or requirements, with a bar on quantities unreasonably disproportionate to a stated estimate or relevant normal levels.

cards.front: How can an order for prompt shipment ordinarily be accepted?
cards.back: By a prompt promise to ship or prompt shipment, unless the offer clearly requires otherwise.

cards.front: What is a shipment of nonconforming goods with timely accommodation notice?
cards.back: A counteroffer rather than acceptance of the order, under the UCC accommodation rule.

cards.front: What is a shipment of nonconforming goods without accommodation notice ordinarily?
cards.back: An acceptance and a breach, subject to the contract and applicable rules.

cards.front: Can an acceptance with extra terms form a UCC contract?
cards.back: Yes, unless acceptance is expressly conditional on assent to those terms.

cards.front: How are extra terms treated when a UCC party is not a merchant?
cards.back: As proposed additions requiring assent to become contract terms.

cards.front: When can extra terms automatically enter a contract between merchants?
cards.back: When the offer does not limit acceptance, the additions are not material, and no timely objection applies.

cards.front: How are conflicting terms under UCC 2-207 treated?
cards.back: Courts differ; many cancel the conflicting terms and use UCC defaults. Check the applicable approach.

cards.front: What terms govern a UCC contract formed by conduct despite incompatible writings?
cards.back: Agreed written terms plus applicable UCC supplementary terms.

cards.front: What is the perfect-tender rule?
cards.back: Subject to exceptions and contract terms, a buyer may reject a single-delivery tender that fails in any respect to conform.

cards.front: What choices does a buyer have under the basic perfect-tender rule?
cards.back: Reject all, accept all, or accept commercial units and reject the rest, subject to good faith and other limits.

cards.front: When is rejection of goods effective?
cards.back: Within a reasonable time after delivery or tender and with timely notice to the seller.

cards.front: What is the seller's ordinary cure right before the delivery deadline?
cards.back: After timely notice, the seller may make a conforming delivery within the contract time.

cards.front: Can a seller sometimes cure after the contract deadline?
cards.back: Yes, where reasonable grounds supported believing the tender acceptable and timely notice is given, the UCC may allow a further reasonable time.

cards.front: What is acceptance of goods under Article 2?
cards.back: Conduct such as signifying acceptance after an inspection opportunity, failing effectively to reject, or acting inconsistently with the seller's ownership.

cards.front: Does accepting goods eliminate every warranty claim?
cards.back: No. A buyer can retain damages claims but must give required notice of breach within a reasonable time.

cards.front: When may a buyer revoke acceptance for defects?
cards.back: When defects substantially impair value and qualifying reliance on cure, difficulty discovering defects, or seller assurances applies.

cards.front: What timing and notice limits apply to revocation of acceptance?
cards.back: It must be timely after discovery or required discovery, precede disqualifying changes in condition, and be communicated to the seller.

cards.front: What is an express warranty under Article 2?
cards.back: A factual affirmation, promise, description, or sample that becomes part of the basis of the bargain.

cards.front: Does ordinary seller puffery necessarily create an express warranty?
cards.back: No. Mere opinion or commendation is generally distinguished from a factual warranty.

cards.front: What is the implied warranty of merchantability?
cards.back: For a merchant seller of goods of that kind, goods must meet ordinary fitness and other statutory merchantability standards.

cards.front: What creates the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
cards.back: The seller has reason to know the buyer's particular purpose and reliance on the seller's judgment, and the buyer actually relies.

cards.front: Must a seller be a merchant for the particular-purpose warranty?
cards.back: No.

cards.front: How is merchantability ordinarily disclaimed in writing?
cards.back: The disclaimer must mention merchantability and be conspicuous, subject to other statutory limits and effective alternatives.

cards.front: How is the implied fitness warranty ordinarily disclaimed?
cards.back: By a conspicuous writing, subject to statutory rules and exceptions.

cards.front: What can an effective as-is clause do?
cards.back: Exclude implied warranties when governing requirements are met; it does not automatically negate express warranties or other protections.

cards.front: When does risk ordinarily pass in a conforming shipment contract?
cards.back: On proper delivery to the carrier, absent contrary agreement or an applicable exception.

cards.front: When does risk ordinarily pass in a conforming destination contract?
cards.back: When the goods are properly tendered at the required destination so the buyer can take delivery.

cards.front: When does risk pass for a merchant seller without a carrier or bailee arrangement?
cards.back: On the buyer's receipt, absent breach, contrary agreement, or another applicable exception.

cards.front: When does risk pass for a nonmerchant seller without a carrier or bailee arrangement?
cards.back: On tender of delivery, absent breach, contrary agreement, or another applicable exception.

cards.front: What is cover under Article 2?
cards.back: A buyer's reasonable, good-faith purchase of substitute goods without unreasonable delay after seller breach.

cards.front: What is the basic buyer cover-damages measure?
cards.back: Cover price minus contract price, plus allowable incidental and consequential losses, minus expenses saved.

cards.front: What is the basic seller resale-damages measure?
cards.back: Contract price minus qualifying resale price, plus allowable incidental losses, minus expenses saved.

cards.front: What is adequate assurance under UCC 2-609?
cards.back: A party with reasonable grounds for insecurity may demand written assurance and, when commercially reasonable, suspend unreturned performance.

cards.front: How long may a UCC adequate-assurance response reasonably take?
cards.back: A reasonable time not exceeding 30 days; failure can amount to repudiation.

cards.front: What is the traditional Article 2 limitations period for a sales-contract action?
cards.back: Four years; parties may reduce it to at least one year but may not extend it by original agreement, subject to applicable law.
